title: Moroccan Harira
subtitle: Moroccan soup with lentils, chickpeas, and lamb
excerpt: Harira is the traditional Moroccan soup eaten to break the fast during Ramadan. It is a thick, warming soup of lentils, chickpeas, lamb, and tomatoes, spiced with cinnamon and coriander. Outside Ramadan, it is eaten year-round as a starter or a main meal.
sourceNotes: Harira is one of Morocco's most iconic dishes. It is the first meal eaten each evening during Ramadan, traditionally paired with dates and sweet pastries. The name comes from the Arabic word for silk, describing the smooth texture of the finished soup.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freezes well for up to 3 months. Reheat gently and add a squeeze of lemon when serving.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the recipe easily for a large batch.

content.text: Harira thickens as it sits. If making ahead, it will need a splash of water to loosen when reheating. A squeeze of fresh lemon juice just before serving brightens the finished soup considerably.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion for 6 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and celery. Cook for 3 more minutes.
Add the beef mince. Break it up with a spoon and cook for 5 minutes until browned.
Add the cumin, coriander, and cinnamon. Stir for 1 minute. Add the tinned tomatoes and 1.5 litres of water. Stir well.
Add the rinsed lentils and salt. Bring to the boil, then reduce to a steady simmer. Cook for 25 minutes.
Add the chickpeas. Simmer for a further 15 minutes until the lentils are completely soft and the soup has thickened.
Taste and adjust salt. Stir in a tablespoon of plain flour mixed with cold water if you want a thicker consistency. Serve with a squeeze of lemon.

items.cause: Lentils did not cook down enough, or too much water was added
items.fix: Mix 2 tbsp plain flour with cold water to a smooth paste and stir in -- simmer for 3 minutes

items.cause: Not enough salt, or spices added too late
items.fix: Season generously and always add spices at the oil stage, not into the water
Simmer for another 15 minutes and cover the pot if needed

content.text: Harira is eaten across Morocco every day during Ramadan, and throughout the year in homes, street food stalls, and restaurants. It is often sold in the evening from large pots in Moroccan medinas. Each family has its own version -- some thicker, some with vermicelli, some with a little tomato paste added for depth.
